data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Sebaceous hyperplasia** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is sebaceous hyperplasia?**
- Common benign enlargement of sebaceous glands around a central dilated follicular duct — 2–6 mm soft yellowish papules with central umbilication (dell) on forehead, cheeks, nose of middle-aged/elderly (UV, ageing — reduced androgen-driven turnover)
- Also: neonatal (maternal androgens — tiny yellow papules on nose; resolve), transplant recipients on cyclosporine, familial premature form, juxtaclavicular beaded lines

**Q2. Discuss the variations of sebaceous glands (PYQ).**
- Ectopic sebaceous glands (not associated with hair follicles): Fordyce spots (lips, buccal mucosa, genitalia), Montgomery tubercles (areola), Tyson's glands (prepuce), Meibomian glands (eyelids), glands of Zeis
- Physiological changes: large in neonates (maternal androgens), small in childhood, enlarge at puberty; reduced in old age
- Disorders: sebaceous hyperplasia, nevus sebaceous, steatocystoma multiplex (cysts with sebaceous lobules in wall — KRT17), sebaceous adenoma/sebaceoma/epithelioma and sebaceous carcinoma (eyelid — aggressive), Muir–Torre syndrome (sebaceous neoplasms + keratoacanthomas + visceral cancers — mismatch repair genes MSH2/MLH1)

**Q3. Dermoscopy and histopathology.**
- Dermoscopy: yellow-white lobular globules ('cumulus clouds/popcorn') with crown vessels that do not cross the centre (vs arborising vessels crossing the BCC surface)
- Histology: enlarged mature sebaceous lobules arranged around a dilated central duct opening to the surface; no atypia

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Nodular BCC (pearly, arborising vessels, slowly growing — biopsy if doubt), sebaceous adenoma (Muir–Torre if multiple/young), molluscum contagiosum, milia, xanthelasma, syringoma, trichoepithelioma, fibrous papule of the nose, colloid milium, rhinophyma (diffuse)

**Q5. When should you think of Muir–Torre syndrome?**
- Sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma or sebaceous carcinoma (not ordinary sebaceous hyperplasia), especially if multiple, outside head and neck, or in younger patients — check mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2) and screen for colorectal and other visceral cancers

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Benign — reassurance
- Light electrodesiccation, cryotherapy, shave excision, curettage, CO2/Er:YAG/pulsed-dye laser, PDT, trichloroacetic acid; oral isotretinoin (low dose) for multiple lesions (relapse after stopping)

**Q7. Describe the Muir–Torre syndrome sebaceous tumours.**
- Sebaceous adenoma (commonest), sebaceoma (sebaceous epithelioma), sebaceous carcinoma, keratoacanthomas with sebaceous differentiation; associated visceral malignancy — colorectal (most), endometrial, urological; MSH2/MLH1 mismatch repair defects — immunohistochemistry loss of MMR proteins in skin tumour; colonoscopy screening

**Q8. What is sebaceous carcinoma?**
- Aggressive adnexal carcinoma, commonest periocular (Meibomian glands — upper eyelid; mimics chalazion/ blepharoconjunctivitis — 'masquerade syndrome'), elderly Asian women; pagetoid spread; metastasis to nodes; treat with wide excision/ Mohs, conjunctival map biopsies; Muir–Torre association

**Q9. Treatment options for sebaceous hyperplasia.**
- Electrodesiccation/ cautery, cryotherapy, CO2 or pulsed-dye laser, photodynamic therapy, trichloroacetic acid, shave excision; oral isotretinoin (low-dose) for multiple lesions (relapse after stopping)

**Q10. Describe the sebaceous gland structure and secretion.**
- Holocrine glands (entire cell disintegrates to release sebum) attached to hair follicles (pilosebaceous unit) except free glands (Fordyce, Meibomian, Tyson's, Montgomery); sebum — triglycerides, wax esters, squalene, cholesterol esters; androgen-dependent

**Q11. Juxta-clavicular beaded lines and other variants.**
- Sebaceous hyperplasia variants: juxta-clavicular beaded lines (parallel rows of papules on neck/clavicles), linear/ diffuse sebaceous hyperplasia, familial premature sebaceous hyperplasia, nevus sebaceous (hamartoma)

**Q12. Describe radiofrequency/ electrosurgery modalities used for benign lesions.**
- Electrodesiccation (monoterminal, superficial dehydration), electrofulguration (sparking, no contact), electrocoagulation (biterminal, deeper), electrosection (cutting — radiofrequency 'radiosurgery' 3–4 MHz gives fine cuts with less thermal damage); precautions — pacemakers (use bipolar), alcohol-based prep (fire), smoke plume (HPV), avoid on keloid-prone skin

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Age-related decrease in androgen levels slows sebocyte turnover → enlarged sebaceous lobules around a dilated duct; also associated with chronic sun damage, cyclosporine (transplant patients), HIV, X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia; premature/familial forms; neonatal (maternal androgens) — yellow papules on nose of newborns

**Q14. Differentiate from BCC clinically and by dermoscopy.**
- Sebaceous hyperplasia: yellowish umbilicated papule with central pore, 'crown vessels' (vessels at the periphery not crossing the centre), cumulus-like yellow lobules ('bunch of popcorn')
- BCC: pearly translucent, arborising vessels crossing the lesion, blue-grey ovoid nests, ulceration

**Q15. What are Fordyce spots?**
- Ectopic sebaceous glands opening directly onto mucosa — vermilion border, buccal mucosa, labia minora, glans/shaft of penis; tiny yellow-white papules; normal variant (Montgomery tubercles on areola, Tyson's glands on penis are related)

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow umbilicated papules on forehead of elderly man — sebaceous hyperplasia (crown vessels)
- Sebaceous adenoma → think Muir–Torre

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Sebaceous gland disorders and tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
